verdict.rationale: The cited verses converge on a settled, knowable confidence whose ground lies outside the believer. In 1 John 5:13 the purpose clause 'so that you may know' (hina eidete) uses the verb 'to know with settled knowledge' (oida, G1492) in the perfect subjunctive (V-RAS-2P, a completed-state form used after 'so that', queried in the source), the verb of settled knowing, governing 'you have' (echete, G2192, present indicative V-PAI-2P, an ongoing simple statement of fact), so the writer's stated aim is that believers may KNOW they presently HAVE eternal life. Romans 8:16 uses 'co-bears witness' (symmartyrei, G4828, present indicative V-PAI-3S, an ongoing simple statement of fact, queried as 1 of only 3 occurrences in the whole Bible), the Spirit co-witnessing with our spirit, an inward ground. Hebrews 10:22 names 'full assurance of faith' (plerophoria pisteos, G4136, full certainty of faith), and 2 Peter 1:10 commands making one's calling and election 'firm' (bebaios, G0949, secure or guaranteed). The three named grounds, the promise, the Spirit's witness, and Spirit-wrought fruit (called 'proven character' or 'tested genuineness' (dokime, G1382)), are each lexically present. The genuine nuance the words leave open is the relative weight of objective promise, inward witness, and evidential fruit, not whether assurance exists.

scripture.force: Queried morphology: 'you may know' (eidete, from oida, G1492) is V-RAS-2P, a perfect-stem subjunctive (a completed-state form used after 'so that') of settled knowing inside the purpose clause 'so that you may know' (hina eidete), and 'you have' (echete, from echo, G2192) is V-PAI-2P, present possession (ongoing simple statement that they currently possess it). The writer's stated aim is that those who believe ('the ones believing' (pisteuousin), present participle, an ongoing-action describing noun-form) may KNOW that they HAVE eternal life ('life eternal' (zoen aionion)) now. The grammar locates assurance in present possession verified by a knowledge verb, not in future attainment or probability.

Queried: 'co-bears witness' (symmartyrei, G4828) is V-PAI-3S (third-person ongoing simple statement of fact) and occurs only 3 times in the whole Bible (Romans 8:16, Romans 9:1, Romans 2:15), each time the 'with' or 'together' prefix (syn-) making the testimony joint and co-attesting. Here the Spirit bears witness WITH our spirit that we are 'children of God' (tekna theou). The near-rare verb is unambiguous in sense, an inward co-witness, which the proposition names as the second ground of assurance.

The aorist (completed past action) passive participle 'having been justified' (dikaiothentes) grounds the indicative 'we have peace toward God' (eirenen echomen pros ton theon). The settled status precedes and produces the relational peace, so assurance rests on an accomplished justification 'out of faith' (ek pisteos). 'To justify' or 'to declare righteous' (dikaioo, G1344) clusters heavily in Romans and Galatians, a stable forensic (courtroom-verdict) sense across the queried distribution.

'We boast in hope of the glory of God' (kauchometha ep elpidi tes doxes tou theou) sets confident hope as the standing posture of those who have 'access' (prosagogen) into this grace. 'Hope' (elpis, G1680) in the queried canon spread denotes confident expectation, not mere wish, so the boasting is forward-looking confidence rather than presumption.

The chain begins 'tribulation produces endurance' (thlipsis hypomonen katergazetai). Suffering is not a counter-witness to assurance but feeds the progression toward proven character. 'Endurance' (hypomone, G5281) carries a stable sense of steadfast endurance across its 32 queried occurrences.

'Endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope' (hypomone dokimen, dokime de elpida). 'Proven character' or 'tested genuineness' (dokime, G1382, queried at 7 occurrences) denotes tested, demonstrated genuineness, the lexical core of Spirit-wrought evidence feeding back into confident hope. Its cognate (a related word from the same root) 'failing the test' or 'disqualified' (adokimos, G0096) names the failed-test outcome, so the same dokim- root (the 'test/prove' word-family) supplies both the evidence of assurance and the standard of self-examination.

'The hope does not put to shame' (he elpis ou kataischynei), grounded in 'the love of God has been poured out in our hearts' (he agape tou theou ekkechytai en tais kardiais hemon) 'through the Holy Spirit' (dia pneumatos hagiou). The perfect tense 'has been poured out' (ekkechytai, a completed action whose result still stands) marks an abiding poured-out state, the inward affective ground of unfailing hope. 'Love' (agape, G0026) here is God's love toward us, the source, not our love as merit.

'Let us draw near in full assurance of faith' (proserchometha en plerophoria pisteos) with 'a true heart' (alethines kardias). 'Full assurance' or 'full certainty' (plerophoria, G4136, queried N-DSF, a noun in the 'in/by/with' grammatical form) occurs only 4 times (Hebrews 10:22, Hebrews 6:11, 1 Thessalonians 1:5, Colossians 2:2) and denotes fullness and complete certainty in every instance. The participles 'having been sprinkled' (rerantismenoi) and 'having been washed' (lelousmenoi) (perfect-tense forms describing completed actions whose results still stand) ground that assurance in an accomplished cleansing.

'Be diligent to make your calling and election firm' (spoudasate bebaian hymon ten klesin kai eklogen poieisthai). 'Firm' or 'secure' (bebaios, G0949, queried A-ASF, an adjective in a particular grammatical form, 8 occurrences including 2 Peter 1:19, Hebrews 3:14, Hebrews 6:19, Romans 4:16) denotes firm, secure, guaranteed. The middle-voice infinitive 'to make' (poieisthai, a verb form where the subject acts on or for itself) casts assurance as something the believer confirms experientially through diligence, the evidential ground, while 'you will never stumble' (ptaisete pote) attaches the promise.

Queried: 'I know' (oida, G1492) here is V-RAI-1S (first-person perfect indicative, a completed-state simple statement of fact), 'I know whom I have believed' (oida ho pepisteuka). The first-person settled-knowledge verb pairs with the perfect 'I have believed' (pepisteuka, a completed action whose result still stands, an enduring state of having believed), so the assurance is personal, present, and grounded in the object of faith. This is the same 'I know' (oida) that 1 John 5:13 makes the writer's aim for all believers.

Queried: 'test yourselves' (heautous peirazete, G3985, V-PAM-2P, second-person plural present command) and 'examine yourselves' (heautous dokimazete, G1381, V-PAM-2P, second-person plural present command) are present imperatives (ongoing commands), test and examine yourselves, with the cognate 'failing the test' or 'disqualified' (adokimoi, G0096) naming the disqualified outcome. The same 'test/prove' root (dokim-) that grounds assurance in Romans 5:4 ('proven character' (dokime), proven) here funds a command to test whether Christ is in you. The text presents assurance and self-examination together, not in opposition.

complicating_texts.resolution: The present imperatives (ongoing commands) 'examine yourselves' (dokimazete) and 'test yourselves' (peirazete) (queried V-PAM-2P, second-person plural present command, test and examine yourselves) with the cognate 'failing the test' or 'disqualified' (adokimoi, G0096, queried at 8 occurrences including 2 Corinthians 13:5, 13:6, 13:7) could be read as making assurance perpetually unsettled. Lexically the same 'test/prove' root (dokim-) grounds assurance in Romans 5:4 ('proven character' or 'tested genuineness' (dokime), proven genuineness) and funds the test here, so the verse does not deny assurance but anchors it in a verifiable reality (whether Christ is in you). The examination is the means by which evidential assurance is confirmed, not a withholding of it.

The command 'be diligent to make firm' (spoudasate bebaian poieisthai) could be read as making assurance contingent on works. Lexically the middle voice 'to make' (poieisthai, a verb form where the subject acts on or for itself) concerns the believer confirming and experiencing an election already grounded in God's prior 'calling' (klesis) and 'choosing' (ekloge), supported by the cross-reference to 2 Timothy 2:19 (the firm foundation stands, the Lord knows those who are his). The verse supports evidential assurance through Spirit-wrought diligence rather than earning the promise.

The hortatory subjunctive 'let us draw near' (proserchometha, a 'let us do X' verb form) is a summons, which could be read as conditional (an 'if-then' arrangement). But 'full assurance of faith' (plerophoria pisteos, full certainty of faith) is presented as the present possession enabling the approach, and the perfect participles (completed actions whose results still stand) 'having been sprinkled' (rerantismenoi) and 'having been washed' (lelousmenoi) anchor it in completed cleansing, so the exhortation presupposes assurance rather than withholding it.

variants.note: The lexical store holds 116 VariantUnit nodes, all within the 3 John CBGM window (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, a textual-criticism tool published only for select books), so none of the cited assurance verses fall in published or shadow CBGM scope. 1 John 5:13 carries known manuscript variation in the relative-clause word order around 'to the ones believing in the name' (tois pisteuousin eis to onoma), but the queried 'so that you may know' (hina eidete) clause that carries the verdict is textually stable, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: assurance grounded chiefly in the objective promise
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Weights 1 John 5:13 ('so that you may know' (hina eidete), the writer's aim that believers KNOW) and 2 Timothy 1:12 ('I know' (oida), I know whom I have believed) as locating assurance primarily in the promise of God received by faith, so that assurance belongs to the essence of believing. The queried perfect-stem 'to know' (oida) (a completed-state knowing-verb) and present 'you have' (echete, an ongoing simple statement of present possession) support reading assurance as a present given rather than a later prize.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: assurance grounded chiefly in the inward witness of the Spirit
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Weights Romans 8:16 'co-bears witness' (symmartyrei) (the Spirit co-witnesses) and Romans 5:5 (the love of God poured out by the Spirit) as the experiential, affective ground. On this reading assurance is felt confirmation, not bare inference from the promise. The queried near-rare 'to co-bear witness' (symmartyreo), always co-attesting, supports a genuinely inward testimony.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: assurance grounded chiefly in Spirit-wrought fruit and self-examination
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Weights 2 Peter 1:10 (make your calling and election 'firm' (bebaios, secure)) and 2 Corinthians 13:5 ('examine yourselves' (dokimazete)) as making assurance a verified reality tested by evidence of a changed life. On this reading assurance can be a distinct attainment that grows with diligence. The shared 'test/prove' root (dokim-) in Romans 5:4 'proven character' (dokime) and 2 Corinthians 13:5 supports an evidential ground, and the queried 'failing the test' or 'disqualified' (adokimos) shows the test can register a negative result.

hermeneutics.notes: The proposition states only that believers MAY have well-grounded assurance founded on three named grounds (the promise, the Spirit's witness, and Spirit-wrought fruit). All three lenses affirm that such assurance exists lexically. They diverge on which ground is primary and on whether assurance is inseparable from faith or a distinct attainment confirmed over time. The vocabulary supports the existence and the three grounds but does not rank them, which is the honest source of legitimate divergence.

stem_audit.notes: The stem uses the modal MAY have and lists three grounds (promises of God, inward witness of the Spirit, Spirit-wrought fruit) that map directly to queried lexical features ('you may know' (eidete) plus 'you have eternal life' (echete zoen aionion) in 1 John 5:13, 'co-bears witness' (symmartyrei) in Romans 8:16, 'proven character' (dokime) in Romans 5:4 and 'firm' (bebaios) in 2 Peter 1:10). It does not embed a tradition-specific taxonomy such as a particular full-assurance-versus-faith-assurance scheme, so it is not verdict-preloaded. The verdict is derived from the words, not the stem.

lay_summary: The verses cited point one way. In 1 John 5:13 the writer states his purpose with 'so that you may know' (hina eidete), built on the word for purpose plus 'to know with settled knowledge' (oida), a verb of settled knowing (here a perfect-stem form, a completed-state form, confirmed by querying the text), and his goal is that people who believe may KNOW they HAVE eternal life right now, using present-tense possession. That is assurance grounded in a promise. In 2 Timothy 1:12 the same verb appears as 'I know' (oida), I know whom I have believed, the personal form of that knowledge. In Romans 8:16 the verb 'co-bears witness' (symmartyrei) means the Spirit bears witness together WITH our spirit that we are children of God. That verb occurs only three times in the whole New Testament and always means a joint, co-attesting testimony, so it names a genuinely inward ground, the witness of the Spirit. Romans 5:1-5 starts from having been justified, which yields peace toward God, then builds a chain: pressure produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope, a hope that does not put us to shame because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts. The word 'proven character' or 'tested genuineness' (dokime) describes tested, demonstrated genuineness, the third ground, fruit worked by the Spirit. Hebrews 10:22 names 'full assurance of faith' (plerophoria pisteos) outright, a word that means complete certainty and appears only four times, and ties it to a heart already sprinkled and washed. Second Peter 1:10 tells believers to make their calling and election 'firm' (bebaios), a word that means guaranteed. One verse pulls the other way: Second Corinthians 13:5 commands 'examine yourselves' (dokimazete), using the same 'test/prove' root that elsewhere means proven, and warns of being 'disqualified' (adokimos, failing the test). But that command tests a reality, it does not deny that assurance exists. So across an apostle, two letters of Paul, and Hebrews the same picture holds: believers may rest in a confidence anchored in the promise, the Spirit's witness, and visible fruit. What the words do not settle is which of those three grounds weighs most, or whether assurance is built into faith from the start or grows as a separate confidence over time. That open question, not any doubt about whether assurance exists, is where careful readers honestly diverge. The pattern is consistent and the verdict affirms the proposition.
